bp: The paper starts from a very practical web-platform problem: a conference has many papers and many reviewers, and every paper must be assigned to someone. These assignments are chores, because reading and evaluating a paper consumes time. But the same paper is not equally painful for every reviewer. If a reviewer bid on a paper, the model treats that assignment as carrying no cost for that reviewer, because the reviewer has already signaled interest or fit. If the reviewer did not bid on it, the paper carries its inherent cost, such as the effort implied by its length. The platform therefore wants two things at once. It wants low total burden across all reviewers, and it wants no reviewer to be stuck with a bundle that looks plainly worse than someone else's. The paper studies this as fair resource allocation, where the resource being allocated is unwanted work rather than a prize.
wh: The difficulty is that fairness and efficiency pull against each other. If the platform only minimizes total effort, it might give every bid-on paper to interested reviewers and dump the remaining costly papers on a few people. The total cost could look good while the workload feels unacceptable. If the platform only equalizes the number of papers, it ignores the fact that one long or unwanted paper can be more burdensome than several easy ones. The model is also sharply two-valued for each reviewer-paper pair: the cost is either zero or the full inherent cost. That makes local reasoning dangerous, because an assignment that is free for one reviewer may be expensive for another. The paper must satisfy EFX, meaning envy should disappear after removing any single chore from the envied bundle, and MMS, meaning each reviewer should receive a burden no worse than a reasonable fair-share benchmark. It must do this while keeping total cost near the best possible.
naive: A smart beginner might first sort papers by cost and spread the expensive ones evenly, or assign each paper to someone who bid on it whenever possible. Each rule handles only one part of the problem. Spreading expensive papers evenly ignores that an expensive paper may be free for a bidder and costly for everyone else. Greedily honoring bids can lower total cost, but it may leave a small set of unwanted papers to be concentrated on unlucky reviewers. Equal paper counts fail for the same reason: counts do not measure burden. The hard part is choosing a whole assignment where each reviewer's bundle is fair when judged by cost, while the platform still avoids unnecessary total effort.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat the review assignment as a chore-allocation problem with a very specific cost shape. Each paper has one inherent cost, and each reviewer either pays zero for it because they bid on it or pays that inherent cost because they did not. This restricted additive cost model keeps the problem structured enough for a provable algorithm, while still matching the review-platform story. The algorithm is designed to output an allocation that satisfies two fairness tests at the same time: EFX and MMS. It also controls efficiency by proving that the total social cost, meaning the sum of all reviewers' incurred costs, is at most twice the best possible social cost. The abstract also says this factor of two is optimal for the guarantee being sought, so the result is not merely an arbitrary bound but the best approximation ratio possible under the stated model.
mech: The input is a set of reviewers, a set of papers, an inherent cost for each paper, and bid information saying which reviewer-paper pairs should have zero cost. From this, the system can compute what every possible assignment would cost each reviewer: zero if the reviewer bid on that paper, otherwise the paper's inherent cost. The algorithm then has to choose a partition of the papers, one bundle per reviewer. For each candidate bundle, costs add up across papers, because the model is additive: a reviewer's burden is the sum of the costs of the papers assigned to that reviewer. The mechanism must keep three checks visible while it builds or searches for an allocation. First, it checks EFX: if one reviewer compares their own burden with another reviewer's bundle after any single chore is removed from that other bundle, the comparison should not reveal unacceptable envy. Second, it checks MMS: each reviewer should do at least as well as their maximin-share benchmark, the level they could guarantee by dividing the chores into bundles while expecting to receive the worst bundle. Third, it tracks social cost, the total incurred effort across everyone. The output is one assignment of all papers to reviewers that meets EFX and MMS and whose total cost is within a factor of two of the minimum possible total cost.
math: The main mathematical object is an allocation table. Rows are reviewers, columns are papers, and each cell has a cost: either zero or the paper's inherent cost. Choosing an allocation means selecting exactly one reviewer for each paper, then adding the selected cell costs reviewer by reviewer and in total. This is matching and allocation math: the question is not whether one paper fits one reviewer in isolation, but which whole arrangement of pairings works together. The fairness math supplies two tests. MMS, maximin share, imagines a reviewer splitting all chores into bundles and then receiving the worst bundle; it is a way to define a fair burden without assuming everyone has identical costs. EFX, envy-free up to any chore, asks whether another person's bundle would still look better after removing a single item, so it prevents fairness from depending on one unusually costly chore. The efficiency math is approximation: because perfect minimum social cost may conflict with fairness, the algorithm proves a ratio against the best possible social cost. A 2-approximation means the total burden is no more than twice that best cost, and the abstract says no better ratio is possible here. The tradeoff is fairness versus total effort.
dots: This paper sits in the conference's fair resource allocation thread, but it also connects to matching and efficiency. Like recommendation or expert-routing papers, it asks who should be paired with what under limits; unlike ordinary recommendation, the assigned object is work that must be covered, not an item a user may simply ignore. It also connects to optimization, because the system must define what counts as costly and then search for an arrangement that reduces that cost while obeying fairness rules. The local data also contains another WWW 2026 chore-allocation paper, All-but-one MMS Allocation for Chores, which studies what happens when exact MMS-style fairness cannot be fully achieved and one relaxes the guarantee. This paper takes a different path: under restricted additive costs, it aims to achieve EFX and MMS together, then measures the efficiency price through a provably optimal factor-two social-cost bound. The shared deeper problem is how a platform can allocate unavoidable burdens without sacrificing trust.
ww: The reason the approach can work is that the restricted cost structure gives the algorithm useful order. In a completely arbitrary chore problem, every reviewer might experience every paper with unrelated costs, making fairness comparisons messy. Here, each paper has one inherent cost, and bids only switch that cost off for particular reviewers. That means the algorithm can reason about assignments using a clear map of free versus costly pairings. Bids help efficiency because assigning a paper to a bidder avoids effort that another reviewer would incur. But bids alone are not enough, so the fairness conditions stop the algorithm from concentrating the remaining costs on a few reviewers. MMS anchors each person's burden to a fair-share baseline, while EFX checks the more immediate human complaint: whether someone else's bundle would still look preferable after discounting any one chore. The approximation result explains the price of satisfying those fairness rules. The paper does not claim to always reach the absolute lowest total cost; it claims the unavoidable extra burden can be bounded, and that this bound is the best possible for this setting.
po: The payoff is a stronger assignment rule for platforms that must distribute unwanted tasks. In the motivating review-platform example, it gives a way to use reviewer bids to reduce wasted effort without letting efficiency alone decide who gets the hard leftover papers. The stated result buys simultaneous EFX and MMS fairness, plus a total-cost guarantee within twice the optimum, with that factor shown to be optimal. The abstract also adds a practical note: if polynomial running time is required, slightly weaker fairness guarantees are available. So the contribution is both conceptual and algorithmic: it identifies a structured chore model and shows exactly what combination of fairness, efficiency, and computational demands can be achieved.
limits: The claims depend on the restricted additive cost model being a good description of the real platform. In practice, a bid may not mean zero effort; it may mean interest, expertise, or strategic behavior. Paper cost may also involve more than length, and reviewer capacity constraints are not described in the abstract. The abstract states the existence of an algorithm, fairness guarantees, a factor-two social-cost approximation, optimality of that ratio, and weaker polynomial-time guarantees, but it does not give implementation details, empirical review-assignment results, or evidence about strategic bidding. The result should therefore be read as a mathematical guarantee for the stated model, not proof that every real conference assignment process will be fair in practice.
